artists.biography: Curtis Ousley (February 7, 1934 - August 13, 1971), who performed under the name King Curtis, was an American tenor, alto, and soprano saxophonist who played rhythm and blues, soul, rock, and soul jazz.  Curtis was born in Fort Worth, Texas. During the 1950s and early to mid 1960s he both worked as a session player on such records as Yakety Yak and recorded his own singles. His best known singles from this period are "Soul Twist" (Enjoy) and "Soul Serenade" (Capitol). In 1965 he moved to Atlantic Records, where his most successful singles were "Memphis Soul Stew" and "Ode to Billie Joe." He led Aretha Franklin's backup band, The Kingpins, and produced records, at first with Jerry Wexler and then by himself.  Curtis guested on John Lennon's Imagine and was capable of attracting the best session musicians to put in appearances for his own albums, including Eric Clapton, guitarist Duane Allman on Instant Groove, and organist Billy Preston and drummer Bernard Purdie on Live At Fillmore West.    On Saturday August 13 1971 he was stabbed outside his apartment and pronounced dead upon arrival at hospital.

perplexity.description:
King Curtis’s Live at Fillmore West, originally released in 1971, captures the energy and virtuosity of one of soul and jazz’s most influential saxophonists at the peak of his powers. Recorded with his band the Kingpins at the legendary San Francisco venue, the album blends jazz, funk, and soul into a dynamic live set. Curtis’s commanding tenor saxophone leads the way, supported by tight arrangements and a rhythm section that effortlessly bridges the worlds of jazz improvisation and soulful groove. The performance features a mix of original compositions and covers, highlighting Curtis’s ability to infuse each tune with both technical brilliance and emotional depth.

This album stands as a pivotal entry in King Curtis’s discography, representing his transition from session sideman to bandleader and showcasing his unique ability to unite jazz sophistication with the raw energy of funk and soul. Released on ATCO Records, Live at Fillmore West was well-received for its vibrant sound and masterful musicianship, cementing Curtis’s reputation as a live performer. The album’s success helped bridge the gap between jazz and popular music audiences, and it remains a celebrated example of early 1970s soul jazz.
